title: Working into the bottom loop only
subtitle: How inserting the hook into the lower loop of a stitch changes the fabric texture
excerpt: Working into the bottom loop of a stitch is less common than back or front loop, but it produces a flat, ribbed texture that suits borders and bands.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: The lower of the two loops at the top of a stitch, sitting between the front and back loops when the stitch is viewed from the front.
The loop at the top of a stitch that sits closest to you when the work faces you.
The loop at the top of a stitch that sits furthest from you when the work faces you. Working into it leaves the front loop free as a horizontal ridge.

content.text: of a stitch means inserting the hook into the third, lower loop that sits below the standard

. This leaves both top loops free and visible, creating a ridged, fabric-like texture. It appears most often in ribbed borders, slouch-hat brims, and flat bands where a dense, structured look is wanted.

The bottom loop is only clearly visible on tall stitches: half treble and above. On a half treble, look at the top of the post. There are three loops: the two standard top-of-stitch loops (front and back) and a lower one that runs horizontally across the front just below them. That lower one is the bottom loop.
At the top of the stitch, identify the two standard loops (the V on top) and the lower horizontal loop below them.
Insert the hook into that lower loop only, passing below both top loops.
Work the stitch as normal from that insertion point.
The two unworked top loops remain visible as a raised horizontal bar on the fabric face.

items.symptom: The bottom loop cannot be found
items.cause: The bottom loop is most visible on half trebles and taller stitches. It is very hard to see on short stitches like double crochet.
items.fix: Check the stitch type. If the pattern calls for bottom-loop work in double crochet, this may be a misprint. The technique is almost always applied to half trebles.

items.symptom: The fabric is pulling tighter than expected
items.cause: The hook is entering below two loops rather than one, which reduces the stitch head and tightens each stitch.
items.fix: Go up half a hook size, or ease the draw-up loop slightly taller when working into the bottom loop.

content.text: Work a short swatch in half trebles, alternating one row of standard top-loops with one row of bottom-loop only, to see how the texture builds up across several rows. The resulting fabric closely resembles a ribbed band.
